props.title: Thank You for Smoking
props.initialSlug: A lobbyist spins tobacco's deadly truth into gold

sections.content: Thank You for Smoking (2005) brilliantly skewers the art of spin through tobacco lobbyist Nick Naylor's shameless defense of cigarettes. Aaron Eckhart's magnetic performance channels the same corporate satire energy that made Network (1976) and Glengarry Glen Ross (1992) classics, but with a distinctly post-millennial cynicism. Director Jason Reitman crafts a wickedly funny takedown of PR manipulation while avoiding the obvious moral high ground - this isn't an anti-smoking PSA, it's an exploration of how language and rhetoric can defend literally anything.

movies.slug: TV news anchor's mental breakdown becomes ratings gold in this prescient media satire

sections.content: The film belongs to a sharp wave of mid-2000s corporate satires like Lord of War (2005) and Syriana (2005) that examined how skilled talking heads could justify global misdeeds. But where those films took darker dramatic approaches, Reitman maintains a lighter touch that makes the medicine go down easier while still landing its punches. The film's structure, following Naylor as he spins for Big Tobacco on talk shows and teaches his son the art of argumentation, creates a fascinating father-son story about passing down the tools of moral flexibility.

What sets Thank You for Smoking apart is how it avoids becoming preachy while dissecting the mechanics of modern spin. Like Vice (2018) and The Big Short (2015), it pulls back the curtain on institutional corruption with wit rather than rage. The film's "MOD Squad" (Merchants of Death) meetings between tobacco, alcohol and firearms lobbyists provide some of the most cutting commentary on how industries collaborate to normalize harmful products. sections.content: The film launched a new era of smart satires about professional liars, paving the way for works like Miss Sloane (2016) and I Care A Lot (2020). These films share a fascination with articulate antiheroes who weaponize rhetoric and logic to defend the indefensible. The casting of Aaron Eckhart proves crucial - his square-jawed charm and absolute conviction make Naylor's arguments almost seductive, forcing viewers to examine why we're sometimes swayed by clearly unethical positions when they're wrapped in compelling rhetoric.
